questions.problem: Consider two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with expectations $\text{E}[X]=1,$ $\text{E}[Y]=3,$ mixed moment $\text{E}[XY]=2,$ and second raw moments $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=2$ and $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]=15.$ Find the variance of $4X+3Y.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =2-{1}^{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =15-{3}^{2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =2-1\cdot 3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[4X+3Y] & ={4}^{2}\cdot 1+{3}^{2}\cdot 6+2\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot (-1) \\  & =16+54-24 \\  & =46.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\text{Var}[3X+4Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.15$ | $0.45$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.2$ | $0.35$ | $0.55$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.45+4\cdot 0.55 \\  & =2.2\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.45+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.55 \\  & =8.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =8.8-{2.2}^{2} \\  & =3.96.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.5-{1.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+4\cdot 1\cdot f(4,1)+4\cdot 2\cdot f(4,2) \\  & =0+0+4\cdot 0.2+8\cdot 0.35 \\  & =3.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =3.6-2.2\cdot 1.5 \\  & =0.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X+4Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 3.96+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 0.3 \\  & =35.64+4+7.2 \\  & =46.84.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.7 \\  & =0.7\end{aligned}

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.3+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.7 \\  & =0.7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =0.7-{0.7}^{2} \\  & =0.21.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot f(0,0)+0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+1\cdot 0\cdot f(1,0)+1\cdot 1\cdot f(1,1) \\  & =0+0+0+1\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.5-0.7\cdot 0.7 \\  & =0.01.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[4X+2Y] & ={4}^{2}\cdot 0.21+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.21+2\cdot 4\cdot 2\cdot 0.01 \\  & =3.36+0.84+0.16 \\  & =4.36.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For three random variables ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3},$ we have the following variances and covariances:

$$
\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]=2,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]=5,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{3}]=3\,
$$

$$
\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]=4,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]=1,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}]=3\,
$$

Find $\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},…,{X}_{n}$ are random variables, and ${a}_{1},…,{a}_{n}$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{X}_{i}]={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{i}]+2{\sum }_{i<j}{a}_{i}{a}_{j}\text{Cov}[{X}_{i},{X}_{j}].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables and constants ${a}_{1}={a}_{2}={a}_{3}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}] & =\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+\text{Var}[{X}_{3}] \\  & +2\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]+2\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]+2\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}] & =2+5+3+2\cdot 4+2\cdot 1+2\cdot 3=26.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For three random variables ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3},$ we have the following variances and covariances:

$$
\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]=4,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]=2,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{3}]=1\,
$$

$$
\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]=1,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]=2,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}]=3\,
$$

Find $\text{Var}[2{X}_{1}-{X}_{2}-3{X}_{3}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},…,{X}_{n}$ are random variables, and ${a}_{1},…,{a}_{n}$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{X}_{i}]={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{i}]+2{\sum }_{i<j}{a}_{i}{a}_{j}\text{Cov}[{X}_{i},{X}_{j}].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables, we have the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3}] & ={a}_{1}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+{a}_{2}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+{a}_{3}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{3}] \\  & +2{a}_{1}{a}_{2}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]+2{a}_{1}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]+2{a}_{2}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2{X}_{1}-{X}_{2}-3{X}_{3}] & ={2}^{2}\cdot 4+(-1)^{2}\cdot 2+(-3)^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & +2\cdot 2\cdot (-1)\cdot 1+2\cdot 2\cdot (-3)\cdot 2+2\cdot (-1)\cdot (-3)\cdot 3 \\  & =16+2+9-4-24+18 \\  & =17.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Variance of a Sum or Difference of Random Variables
canonical_examples.problem: For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\textrm{Var}[X] = 3,$ $\textrm{Var}[Y] = 0.24,$ and $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 0.2.$ Determine $\textrm{Var}[X-Y].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables, then

$$
\textrm{Var}[X \pm Y] = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y] \pm 2\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\textrm{Var}[X - Y] = 3 + 0.24 - 2 \cdot 0.2 = 2.84.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\textrm{Var}[X] = 5,$ $\textrm{Var}[Y] = 2,$ and $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 3.$ Find $\textrm{Var}[2X - 5Y].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX + bY] = a^2\textrm{Var}[X] + b^2\textrm{Var}[Y] + 2ab\,\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2X-5Y] & ={2}^{2}\cdot 5+(-5)^{2}\cdot 2+2\cdot 2\cdot (-5)\cdot 3 \\  & =20+50-60 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating a Combined Variance Given Some Moments
canonical_examples.problem:
The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.4$ | $0.2$ |

Find $\textrm{Var}[5X+2Y].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX+bY] = a^2 \textrm{Var}[X] + b^2 \textrm{Var}[Y] + 2ab\,\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2,
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | $f_X$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.4$ | $0.2$ | $0.6$ |
| $f_Y$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\textrm{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space $S_X,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.6 \\  & =1.8\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.6 \\  & =5.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =5.4-{1.8}^{2} \\  & =2.16.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space $S_Y,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =0\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2-{1}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\textrm{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot f(0,0)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+3\cdot 0\cdot f(3,0)+3\cdot 2\cdot f(3,2) \\  & =0+0+0+6\cdot 0.2 \\  & =1.2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.2-1.8\cdot 1 \\  & =-0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5X+2Y] & ={5}^{2}\cdot 2.16+{2}^{2}\cdot 1+2\cdot 5\cdot 2\cdot (-0.6) \\  & =54+4-12 \\  & =46.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Variance of a Sum of Three Random Variables
canonical_examples.problem:
For three random variables $X_1,X_2,$ and $X_3,$ we have the following variances and covariances:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X_1] = 1,   \qquad
\textrm{Var}[X_2] = 3,   \qquad
\textrm{Var}[X_3] = 8   \qquad
$$

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_2] = 2,   \qquad
\textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_3] = 4,   \qquad
\textrm{Cov}[X_2,X_3] = -5   \qquad
$$

Find $\textrm{Var}[5X_1 + 2X_2 + 3X_3].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ are random variables, and $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ are constants, then

$$
\textrm{Var}\left[\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i X_i \right]
= \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \textrm{Var}[X_i] + 2\sum\limits_{i <     j} a_i a_j \textrm{Cov}[X_i,X_j].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3}] & ={a}_{1}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+{a}_{2}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+{a}_{3}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{3}] \\  & +2{a}_{1}{a}_{2}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]+2{a}_{1}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]+2{a}_{2}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+3{X}_{3}] & ={5}^{2}\cdot 1+{2}^{2}\cdot 3+{3}^{2}\cdot 8 \\  & +2\cdot 5\cdot 2\cdot 2+2\cdot 5\cdot 3\cdot 4+2\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot (-5) \\  & =25+12+72+40+120-60 \\  & =209.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Given two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the variance of the sum or difference of these variables is given by

$$
\textrm{Var}[X\pm Y] = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y] \pm 2\textrm{Cov}[X,Y],
$$

where $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ We'll prove this formula at the end of the lesson.

Note that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]= 0,$ and we have

$$
\textrm{Var}[X\pm Y] = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y].
$$

tutorials.name: The Variance of a Sum of Scaled Random Variables
tutorials.problem:
If $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX + bY] = a^2 \textrm{Var}[X] + b^2 \textrm{Var}[Y] + 2ab \textrm{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 0,$ and we recover the formula

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX + bY] = a^2 \textrm{Var}[X] + b^2 \textrm{Var}[Y] .
$$

tutorials.name: Generalizing to Multiple Random Variables
tutorials.problem:
Finally, we have the following generalization for the variance of a sum of $n$ random variables.

$$
\textrm{Var} \left[ \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i X_i \right] = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \textrm{Var}[X_i] + 2\sum\limits_{i < j} a_i a_j \textrm{Cov}[X_i, X_j]
$$

Let's see an example of how this works in practice.

tutorials.name: Proof of the Sum Formula
tutorials.problem:
Let's prove the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X+ Y] = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y] + 2\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]
$$

Applying the definition of variance and using the linearity of expectation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X+Y] & =\text{E}[((X+Y)-\text{E}[X+Y])^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[((X-\text{E}[X])+(Y-\text{E}[Y]))^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}+(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}+2(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])].\end{aligned}
$$

Distributing the expected value, and using the fact that $\textrm{E}[aX] = a\cdot \textrm{E}[X]$ for constant $a,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X+Y] & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}+(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}+2(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])] \\  & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}]+\text{E}[(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}]+2\cdot \text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])] \\  & =\text{Var}[X]+\text{Var}[Y]+2\text{Cov}[X,Y]\end{aligned}
$$

as required. 

The proof for the difference between two random variables is similar.
